extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in moral philosophy, character, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the qualities Emerson describes as constitutive of 'character' and 'manners' — the moral, social, and aesthetic traits that make a person influential, trustworthy, and gentlemanly. Useful for reading, literary analysis, or reflecting on personal conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as presence / reserved force
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is 'a reserved force which acts directly by presence, and without means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson explains that this element acts by 'presence' rather than by recourse to arguments or outward deeds; it is a magnetism that alters affairs simply by the person's arrival. Examples: Lord Chatham, Washington, Hercules—their presence conveyed authority beyond enumerated acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent power beyond achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest part of some men's power is 'latent' — their reputation outruns the record of deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fame may exceed documented acts because character contains an expectation or intrinsic quality not captured by facts. This latent quality justifies reverence even when deeds are few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness / power to make talent trusted
rubrics_metrics.description: People need in their representative 'much more than talent, namely the power to make his talent trusted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person of character instills faith in others; constituents believe such a person intuitively and accept their words and actions as authoritative without constant proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment / being the thing represented
rubrics_metrics.description: The great person 'is himself the country which he represent[s]'; he embodies the constituency or principle he speaks for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons do not merely advocate opinions; they personify them. Their emotions and opinions are 'instant and true' and thus become a mirror for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of fronting the fact / directness
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic habit is 'fronting the fact, and not dealing with it at second hand, through the perceptions of somebody else.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes firsthand perception and action rather than mediated opinion—direct engagement with reality rather than borrowed impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural probity and reference to natural equity
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural merchant's 'probity combines with his insight into the fabric of society' and he refers 'to standards of natural equity and public advantage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrity anchored in universal standards, producing trustworthiness in trade and public dealings; not merely legal compliance but adherence to natural justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural aptitude / born disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Some faculties are innate: 'a man must be born to trade or he cannot learn it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson asserts that certain social and vocational powers arise from nature; effort alone cannot wholly substitute for native bent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence that overpowers by benumbing resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher natures 'overpower lower ones by affecting them with a certain sleep'—their presence enervates resistance and commands assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character can render others passive or receptive, producing effects analogous to a natural force that flows from the superior to the inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and justice as foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Truth is the summit of being; justice is the application of it to affairs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson locates character in the alignment with truth and the application of that truth as justice; moral authority rests on these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral order / purity of element
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is 'this moral order seen through the medium of an individual nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character reflects an internal moral structure; individuals vary in degree according to the 'purity of this element' in them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured by resistance of circumstances / steadfastness
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'natural measure of this power is the resistance of circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True character is evident in how a person stands against adverse circumstances rather than how they act when conditions are favorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle-centeredness versus event-worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Impure men 'consider life as it is reflected in opinions, events, and persons' whereas men of character see the moral element antecedent to events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of those who chase outcomes; character holds to principles regardless of transient events and refuses to be swayed by popularity or circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectitude as habitual serenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectitude is 'a perpetual victory, celebrated not by cries of joy but by serenity, which is joy fixed or habitual.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral rightness expresses itself as an enduring calm rather than episodic triumph; a sign of genuine character is composed, constant goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficingness / centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: The face of character is 'self-sufficingness'—a sense of mass and centrality that makes a person seem perpetual patron and benefactor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character gives the impression that a person is not easily displaced; society should feel the substantial presence of such persons rather than mere manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonconformity / independence of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Character 'does not accept the conventional opinions and practices'—nonconformity is a goad and remembrancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence from prevailing fashion or opinion is itself a mark of moral force and stimulates inquiry in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action grounded in substance / realistic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Our action 'should rest mathematically on our substance'—attempt nothing beyond one's real capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes congruence between capacity and enterprise; grand pretensions unsupported by inner substance result in tentative, uninspiring action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incessant growth / openness to development
rubrics_metrics.description: A trait of life and character is 'the notice of incessant growth'—men should make us feel a controlling happy future opening before them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character includes continual self-improvement and an orientation toward future development rather than static achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking redemption: new actions justify old
rubrics_metrics.description: 'New actions are the only apologies and explanations of old ones'—the noble remedy past faults by future deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson values active forward motion: restoration and explanation of past failings come through subsequent constructive acts, not apologies alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence as disposition rather than enumerated acts
rubrics_metrics.description: True charity 'is to be inferred' from character, not from a list of donations; love is 'inexhaustible' and not measured by enumerated deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques counting philanthropic acts as the test of goodness; genuine benevolence is habitual and intrinsic, not just recordable transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness / non-artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: This masterpiece (character) is best 'where no hands but nature's have been laid on it' and 'it is of no use to ape it or to contend with it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity is paramount; forced or manufactured displays of character or virtue fail to convince and lack moral efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for perspective / avoid hasty judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Character 'wants room; must not be crowded on by persons nor be judged from glimpses'—it 'needs perspective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of character requires time and broad observation; snap judgments from isolated incidents are misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as mutual self-assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Profound friendship is 'two virtuous men, each of whom is sure of himself and sure of his friend.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest interpersonal relation arises when both parties possess character and mutual confidence; such relations postpone lesser gratifications and make social structures 'cheap.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine person / prophecy of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'divine person is the prophecy of the mind' and represents a high, exemplar moral force that crowds out skepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson elevates exemplary persons as anticipations of moral possibility; they function as social and spiritual exemplars, transforming perception and hope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman as truth-bearing autonomous agent
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman is 'a man of truth, lord of his own actions, and expressing that lordship in his behavior, not in any manner dependent and servile.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners rooted in autonomy and truth, not servility or mere external polish. The gentleman manifests inner lordship through comportment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manhood first, then gentleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners embody 'manhood first, and then gentleness'—strength accompanied by benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True civility combines moral strength with kindness; politeness without substance is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners as surface of deeper qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners are 'the flower and fruit, not the grain of the tree'—an outward manifestation of inner character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson warns that fashion and mere etiquette can masquerade as manners; genuine manners arise from virtue, wit, beauty, wealth, and power combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentility as collective product of virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentility 'is made of the spirit, more than of the talent of men' and is a compound of 'virtue, wit, beauty, wealth, and power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social refinement emerges from an ensemble of excellent traits rather than a single accomplishment; it is a spontaneous fruit of active, leading forces in society.
